Last month, I started a new job at a small company.
I was excited but also nervous.
It was my first office job, and I didn't know anyone there yet.
I woke up early on my first day.
I chose my clothes carefully and left home with plenty of time.
I didn't want to be late on my very first day at a new place.
I arrived at the building twenty minutes early.
But the front door was locked, and there was a keypad next to it.
I didn't have a code, so I just stood outside and waited in the cold morning air.
A few minutes later, another person walked up to the door.
She looked at me and asked if I was new.
I said yes, and she smiled and told me her name was Ana.
Ana worked in a different department, but she showed me how to use the keypad.
She also told me she remembered her own first day very well.
She said everyone feels nervous at first, even people who look calm.
We walked in together, and she took me to the front desk.
The receptionist called my manager, and I waited on a small couch near the window.
My hands felt a little cold, and my heart was beating fast.
My manager came out a few minutes later.
His name was Mr. Chen, and he had a friendly smile.
He shook my hand and said welcome to the team, in a warm and easy voice.
He showed me my desk, my computer, and the kitchen area.
He introduced me to a few coworkers, but I forgot most of their names right away.
There were too many new faces at once, and my brain felt full.
At lunch, Ana found me again.
She asked if I wanted to eat with her and a few others.
I said yes, and we talked about the company and the city while we ate.
By the end of the day, I felt much better.
The morning had felt strange and slow, but the afternoon felt normal.
I even remembered three new names by the time I left the office.
I walked home that evening and thought about the day.
It didn't start the way I planned, but it ended well.
Sometimes the hardest part of something new is just the first hour, not the whole day.
Now, when new people join my team, I always try to help them the way Ana helped me.
I remember how it feels to stand outside a locked door on your first day, alone and unsure.
